newsitem.title: USA: U.S. chemical industry sees favorable 1997.
newsitem.headline: U.S. chemical industry sees favorable 1997.

text.p: The overall outlook for the U.S. chemical industry appeared favorable for 1997, and companies could benefit from unusually strong profit growth, according to a chemical industry trade association.
U.S. chemical companies with annual sales both over and under $1 billion expect profits to grow 10 percent in 1997 from 1996, the Chemical Manufacturers Association said.

They also expected sales, in dollar terms, to grow five percent in 1997, the association said. The United States is the world's largest producer of chemicals, while Germany is the world's largest exporter.

Sales, by volume, were projected to grow by a median 4.7 percent in that period, the group said. Based on the parallel revenue and volume changes in 1997, the group said companies expected overall prices would remain flat compared with 1996.
The chemical companies projected exports would rise six percent in 1997, the group said.

The chemical industry was expected to be the country's number one exporter in 1996, with projected year-end total exported chemical products worth $61.4 billion, Allan Lenz, the association's chief economist, said.

Longer term, slower U.S. economic growth and a maturing U.S. market for chemicals, especially in the housing and automotive sectors, would limit the growth of the U.S. chemical market, the association said. The industry would have to look abroad, to less developed countries, for growth and exports.
"The export growth markets of the future are clearly in the fast-growth developing countries, particularly Asia and Latin America," the CMA said.

"Most of these countries are not only experiencing economic growth rates of six, eight or 10 percent annually, but have chemical needs that expand at 1.6 to 1.8 percent or more for each one percent of economic growth," it said.
Developing countries' chemical consumption typically increases at a pace two or more times their economic growth rates, the association said.
